source.title: Fool's Gold: Defensive Deception Against Safety-Removal Attacks on Open-Weight Models

page_placements.theme: Robustness to direction-based removal: training against ablation, decoys, hidden switches, and removal routes that bypass the direction

record.file_problem: Whole paper is present (4414 lines, main text plus Appendices A-S). The text is a two-column PDF extraction. Some paragraphs (Sec. II-D, VII-C, Appendix H/I) have interleaved or scrambled lines, and Tables I, II, III, XII, XIV, XVI are flattened. Row alignment for the Table II and Table XIV values used here was cross-checked against the text and the delta arithmetic. Figures are only partly legible.
record.tranche_reason: The paper is a defence (decoy hardening) built on top of abliteration, which would normally make it T4. It also applies the original difference-in-means directional ablation (Eq. 2-3) to new models and reports what it did to refusal and compliance. Examples: gemma-3-27b dev refusal 1.00 to 0.00, Qwen3.5-27B/-9B derivation failures, and refusal rates of the attacked undefended models on StrongREJECT/HarmBench slices. Under the T1-first ordering it is T1. The finding that textbook single-direction derivation often fails on current models, while community multi-direction recipes work, also fits T5.
record.gate_note: Not rows: (1) the defence's own results (decoy/fatal rates for defended models, Tables I, VIII, X, XI, XII, XIII, XVI-XVIII, XXV, and the efficacy gates), because they test the new method; (2) the decoy-direction ablation counter-attack and its random-direction control (Tables XXIII-XXIV), which concerns a direction other than refusal; (3) the gate-leakage marker experiment (Table XXI); (4) values used only to choose a layer, direction or acceptance threshold; (5) results cited from other work (Arditi et al., refs 22-25 on cones, categories and harm/refusal separation, ART, DeepRefusal, DDO). The study states that harmfulness is encoded separately from refusal [25] but does not test it.
record.test_reason: A defence paper, but it applies the original difference-in-means ablation (Eq. 2-3) to new models and reports refusal and judged compliance after the attack. Textbook single-direction derivation stripped refusal on gemma-3-27b (1.00 to 0.00) and Qwen3-14B (0.75 to 0.00). It failed on Qwen3.5-27B and -9B, where community or optimizing recipes were needed. Weight forensics of public abliterations and refusal on external benchmark slices for attacked undefended models are also reported. The derivation-failure finding also fits T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors assume abliteration always succeeds and claim no resistance to it; every checkpoint was eventually cracked, and per-checkpoint re-derivation is mandatory. They report that textbook single-direction derivation often fails deceptively on current models (refusal stripped by keyword measures, no judged compliance), while community recipes succeed. They say this is consistent with multi-directional geometry. Caveat: one accepted community recipe (Qwen3.5-27B) is itself a single rank-1 edit.
record.recipe_differences: Same difference-in-means direction at the last prompt token of each layer and weight orthogonalization (Eq. 2-3) for the textbook arm. Direction selection and acceptance use refusal on a dev split plus LLM-judged compliance (gpt-4.1) and a degeneracy check. Main attacks are community or public recipes (heretic-style optimization, banded two-block, expert-granular with router suppression) rather than one global direction. Per-model strongest-found attack, not one fixed recipe. Thinking mode pinned or both. No addition/steering test and no standard capability benchmark after ablation. Targets are Qwen3/3.5, gemma-3/4, gpt-oss, GLM-4.5-Air; the harmful prompts are CBRN-focused.
record.method_sensitivity: Derivation recipe: textbook single-direction derivation worked on gemma-3-27b and Qwen3-14B but not Qwen3.5-27B or -9B, where public-recipe or optimizing derivations were needed (Appendix E). Measure: keyword refusal versus LLM-judged compliance gives different answers (safe-completion collapse). Benchmark slice: Qwen3.5-27B refusal 0.21 on StrongREJECT versus 0.41 on HarmBench (R24, R25). Per-checkpoint re-derivation: a replayed attack gave refusal 1.00 on a later 9B defended checkpoint. Thinking mode is pinned or both. Content judge: GPT-4.1 and the second judges read stricter.

fits_no_version.finding: Compliance-reward GRPO strips refusal without any direction edit: 0.08 (LoRA) and 0.005 (full fine-tune) on defended Qwen3-14B, 0.02-0.06 on the undefended base. Benign SFT after an ablation attack left refusal at 0.0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal can be removed by reward-based fine-tuning without directional ablation, and benign fine-tuning does not restore it.

record.code_released: not stated (the text says code and evaluation harnesses are released but gives no URL)
record.problems: The claim is tested only incidentally. Refusal-removal results for undefended models are mostly one-line statements in Appendix E without sample sizes or CIs; the dev-probe n is not given. The accepted attacks are selected by a search to pass acceptance, so the success rate is a lower bound on attacker capability, not a rate. There is no random-direction control for refusal ablation and no test of adding the direction. Capability after ablation is checked only by a degeneracy prong and a figure-label BioProBench value for one model. The refusal criterion in Table II is not defined in the text read. Table II and Table XIV are flattened and were aligned using cross-checks. Judge-only content scoring (GPT-4.1), partly checked by a single expert. Prompt sets are CBRN-focused and small (50 and 28 prompts for Table II slices).
record.rows_left_out: No rows dropped for the 60-row cap (51 rows kept). Left out because they measure the defence or other behaviours: refusal columns for the attacked defended arms (D0-a) in Table II; fatal, quality and delta columns of Table II; clean-state refusal and utility in Table XII; Table I floors (attacked undefended fatal rates 0.018 to 0.452); per-variant fatal values in Table XXIII; decoy-direction ablation with a random-direction control (Table XXIV); the gate-leakage marker experiment (Table XXI); GRPO fatal rates and GSM8K changes (Tables XIX, XX) except the refusal values kept as R47-R51.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; a random-direction control for the refusal ablation; standard capability benchmarks after ablation (only a degeneracy prong and one BioProBench figure label for Qwen3-14B).
Entirely untested. Jailbreaks are not analysed for direction suppression, and the defence trains decoy expression under simulated ablation, not refusal robustness.
No direct analysis of refusal geometry (cones, affine, category components). Only recipe and edit structure.
Training-stage dependence. The textbook derivation fails on newer models, but the paper does not test why.
The reasoning trace under ablation; adding the direction in reasoning models.

missing.what: Untouched n=100 stratum: attacked-undefended gemma-4-31B and gpt-oss-20b refusals are zero (0.005 in the gpt-oss undefended arm). This is refusal removal on never-touched prompts.

record.verdict_notes: Several V1 links in the record were attached to attacks that are not single-direction (heretic, two-block, router suppression); they are relinked to V2 only. The V3 rows concern defence-trained checkpoints whose training is not refusal-robustness training, so V3 is treated as untested. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Adding the direction to make harmless prompts refused is not tested. There is no random-direction control for the refusal ablation. General capability after ablation is checked only by the attack-acceptance degeneracy prong and one BioProBench figure label for Qwen3-14B.
Only a few attacks are the study's own weight edits. Most are replays or extractions of public abliterated builds, whose release context is not examined.

Whether jailbreaks work by suppressing this direction is not tested. The study trains under simulated ablation for decoy expression, not for refusal robustness. Only in-context jailbreaks are probed, and only for decoy transfer.
No refusal-geometry analysis (cones, affine, category components) of its own. Evidence is indirect: edit structure of public builds and failure of single-direction self-derivation.
Languages and base-to-instruct transfer are not tested. Only original-to-defended fine-tuned variants and defended-checkpoint replays are tested.
Training-stage dependence is not tested. The paper notes textbook derivation works on older models and fails on current-generation ones but does not test why.
Adding the direction in reasoning models is not tested. There is no analysis of the reasoning trace under ablation. Refusal is simply reported after attack with thinking on and off.

reader_labels.reason: Dev refusal fell 1.00 to 0.00 (R01) and 0.75 to 0.00 (R02), and gemma-4-31B judged compliance reached 1.00 (R18). One capability label shows no change on BioProBench (R40), but that is a single model and a figure-only value.

reader_labels.condition: Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-9B, where self-derived single-direction ablation falls short
reader_labels.reason: Self-derived attacks did not pass acceptance: best compliance 0.4375 on 27B (R03), 9B compliance at most 0.25 with refusal never below about 0.25-0.31 (R08, R09). Keyword refusal stripping without judged compliance is also reported (R21), and a 9B reconstruction gave compliance 0.00 (R12). Acceptance needed community recipes. Undefended Qwen3.5-9B/-27B also kept 0.21-0.41 refusal on external benchmark slices (R22-R25).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Accepted community or public-recipe weight edits on seven models: Qwen3.5-27B, -9B, -122B, Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b, gemma-4-31B, GLM-4.5-Air (plus gemma-3-27b)
reader_labels.reason: Every model had an accepted attack (compliance 0.75 to 1.00, refusal 0.00 to 0.20 on dev probes: R06, R10, R13, R14, R15, R17-R20). Undefended attacked models showed near-zero refusal on external slices for 122B, 14B, gpt-oss-20b, gemma-4-31B and GLM-4.5-Air (R26-R35). FORTRESS rubric-met roughly doubled for Qwen3.5-27B and -122B (R36, R37).

reader_labels.reason: Residual refusal of 0.21 to 0.41 on StrongREJECT and HarmBench slices for these two models (R22-R25), and Qwen3.5-27B accepted attack leaves 0.20 refusal (R05). A public-recipe candidate failed the full acceptance conjunction at compliance 0.688 (R04). FORTRESS shows little rise where the clean model already answers (R38, R39).

reader_labels.reason: A fixed replay was blocked after preference round 1, but fresh adaptive derivations were accepted at every checkpoint tried (R41, R43, R46), at rising KL cost 0.295 to 0.628 to 0.877 (R44). The training was not aimed at refusal robustness and the jailbreak half of V3 was not tested.

The authors say this is consistent with multi-directional refusal geometry. The evidence concerns recipes, not a direct geometry analysis.
